b: Density = mass / volume of material (solid, no pores). Bulk density includes pores.
Specific gravity = density of material / density of water at 4°C.
Porosity = volume of voids / total volume × 100.
Water absorption: % weight of water absorbed (by dry weight). Always > 0 for porous solids.
Hygroscopicity: absorbing moisture from air. Permeability: allowing water to pass under pressure.
Frost resistance: depends on density and porosity; dense materials are more frost resistant.
Refractoriness: withstand high temp without melting/deforming (fire bricks).
Fire resistance: withstand fire without losing strength (different from refractoriness).
Elasticity: regain shape on unloading. Plasticity: permanent deformation without cracking.
Ductility: drawn into wires (tension). Malleability: beaten into sheets (compression).
Brittleness: fails suddenly with little deformation (cast iron, glass).
Toughness: energy absorbed up to fracture. Resilience: energy absorbed up to elastic limit.
Hardness: resistance to scratching/indentation — Mohs scale (1 Talc … 10 Diamond).
Creep: increasing strain under constant load over time. Fatigue: failure under repeated loads below ultimate stress.

Mortar = binding material (cement/lime) + fine aggregate + water.
Functions: bind units, distribute load, fill joints, weather-proofing.
Types by binder: cement mortar, lime mortar, gauged mortar (lime + cement), surkhi mortar (surkhi = powdered burnt clay, a pozzolana), mud mortar, gypsum mortar.
Typical cement mortar ratios: masonry 1:4 to 1:6; plaster 1:4 to 1:6; pointing 1:2 to 1:3.
Special: fire-resistant (aluminous cement + fire brick powder), lightweight, sound-absorbing, X-ray shielding (barite), packing mortar.
Lime mortar sets slowly; cement mortar should be used within 30 minutes of adding water.
Exogenous (grow outward, annual rings) — conifers/softwood & deciduous/hardwood. Endogenous (grow inward) — bamboo, palm, cane; not used structurally.
Softwood (conifers): resinous, light colour, distinct annual rings, light weight, non-porous — pine, deodar, chir, fir.
Hardwood (deciduous): dark, close-grained, indistinct rings, heavy, porous — teak, sal, sheesham, oak, mahogany, babul.
Cross-section: pith → heartwood (dead, dark, strong, durable) → sapwood (alburnum — living, light, weaker) → cambium layer → inner bark → outer bark. Medullary rays: radial.
Felling of trees: at maturity; best season — winter (mid-summer in hills) when sap is at rest.
Age of tree = number of annual rings.
Purpose: reduce moisture to ~10–12% (for furniture/joinery 8–10%), prevent decay, shrinkage, warping; increase strength.
Green timber moisture ~ 40–100% or more. Fibre saturation point ~ 25–30%.
Natural: air seasoning (slow, 2–4 years for hardwood), water seasoning.
Artificial: kiln seasoning (fastest, most effective), boiling, chemical (salt) seasoning, electrical seasoning.
Natural: knots (dead/live), shakes (cracks — heart shake, star shake, cup/ring shake, radial shake), twisted fibres, upsets, rind galls, burls, wind cracks.
Seasoning defects: bow, cup, twist, check, split, honeycombing, case hardening, warp.
Conversion defects: chip mark, diagonal grain, torn grain, wane.
Fungi: dry rot (destroys timber into powder, warm damp poorly ventilated places), wet rot (alternate wet & dry). Insects: termites (white ants), beetles, marine borers.
Preservatives: coal tar, creosote oil (most effective oil-type), ASCU (arsenic-copper-chromium; water-borne), chemical salts (zinc chloride, copper sulphate), solignum paint.
Methods: brushing, spraying, dipping & steeping, charring (ends buried in ground), hot & cold open tank, pressure treatment (full-cell Bethell, empty-cell Rueping/Lowry).
Fire retardants: ammonium phosphate, borax, boric acid.
Plywood: thin veneers glued with grain of adjacent layers at right angles; always odd number of plies (3, 5, 7…).
Veneer: thin sheet (0.4–6 mm) of wood cut by rotary cutting, slicing or sawing.
Particle board / chip board (wood chips + resin), fibre board (hard board, insulation board), block board, laminated board, batten board, impreg & compreg timber.
Strength of timber: max in tension along grain; along-grain compressive > across grain. Strongest when loaded parallel to grain.

Varnish: transparent/semi-transparent solution of resin in solvent (oil, spirit, turpentine, water). Types: oil varnish, spirit varnish (French polish = shellac in spirit), turpentine varnish, water varnish, asphalt varnish.

Whitewash: fat lime + water + gum. Colour wash: whitewash + pigment.
Lacquer: cellulose derivative + solvents + plasticisers; quick drying.
Main ingredients: silica (sand) — main; soda/potash (flux, lowers melting point); lime (durability, hardness); cullet (broken glass — helps fusion); colouring agents (metal oxides).

Types: Soda-lime glass (cheapest, windows, bottles), Potash-lime glass (hard glass, fusible at high temp), Potash-lead glass (flint glass — high refractive index; lenses, artificial gems), Borosilicate (Pyrex, low expansion, lab ware), common glass.

Special glass: wired (fire resisting), laminated (safety, shatter-proof — PVB layer), toughened/tempered (heat treated, 4–5 times stronger, breaks into small blunt pieces), tinted, frosted/ground (translucent), glass wool (insulation), fibreglass, structural glass blocks, bullet-proof, photochromatic, ultraviolet.
Annealing of glass: slow cooling to remove internal stresses.
Colouring oxides: Cobalt oxide → blue; Chromium oxide → green; Ferrous → green; Ferric → yellow-brown; Manganese → violet/purple; Cuprous → red; Gold chloride → ruby red; Carbon → amber.
Thermoplastics: soften on heating and harden on cooling repeatedly — PVC, polythene, polystyrene, nylon, acrylic (Perspex), polypropylene, Teflon.
Thermosetting: harden permanently once set; cannot be remoulded — bakelite (phenol-formaldehyde), urea-formaldehyde, epoxy, melamine, polyester.
Properties: light, corrosion resistant, good insulators, easily moulded; but low fire resistance, low stiffness (E), creep, UV degradation.
Uses: PVC pipes, water tanks, laminated sheets, doors/windows (uPVC), adhesives (epoxy), sealants, geo-synthetics.
Bitumen: obtained by fractional distillation of crude petroleum; black/brown, soluble in carbon disulphide (CS₂).
Tar: obtained by destructive distillation of coal or wood; more temperature susceptible; carcinogenic; soluble in toluene.
Asphalt: natural or artificial mixture of bitumen with inert mineral matter (rock asphalt, lake asphalt — e.g. Trinidad lake).
Cutback bitumen: bitumen + volatile solvent — Rapid curing (naphtha/gasoline), Medium curing (kerosene), Slow curing (light oil).
Bitumen emulsion: bitumen dispersed in water with emulsifier; used in wet weather, patch repair.

Tests on bitumen: penetration (grading/hardness — 80/100, 60/70 etc.), ductility (≥ 50–75 cm), softening point (ring & ball), flash & fire point (Pensky-Martens), viscosity, specific gravity, loss on heating, solubility.
Uses: road surfacing, damp-proofing (DPC), waterproofing roofs, joint fillers, felts.
Gypsum (CaSO₄·2H₂O): heating ~120–160°C gives Plaster of Paris (CaSO₄·½H₂O); sets in 5–10 min; used for false ceilings, plaster boards, mouldings.
Keene's cement: anhydrous gypsum + alum; hard, smooth finish plaster.
Pozzolanas: fly ash, surkhi, rice husk ash, silica fume, GGBS, metakaolin — react with Ca(OH)₂ in presence of water.
Asbestos: fibrous mineral; fire resistant; AC (asbestos cement) sheets & pipes — health hazard, now restricted.
Thermal insulating materials: glass wool, mineral/slag wool, cork, vermiculite, thermocol (EPS), asbestos, foam concrete, cellular concrete, air gaps.
Sound absorbing materials: acoustic tiles, fibre board, cork, felt, perforated boards. Sabine's formula: T = 0.16V/A (SI).
Damp-proofing materials: bitumen/asphalt, bituminous felts, plastic sheets (polythene), metal sheets (lead, copper), mortar with waterproofing compounds, stones (slate).
Water-proofing compounds: hydrated lime, calcium chloride, aluminium sulphate, soap, oils, bitumen.
Rubber: natural (latex, hevea tree) — vulcanisation with sulphur improves strength & elasticity.
Adhesives: animal glue, casein, epoxy, phenolic, synthetic resins.
Geosynthetics: geotextiles, geogrids, geomembranes — separation, filtration, reinforcement, drainage.

Concrete = hydraulic cement + aggregates (fine + coarse) + water, with or without admixtures/fibres (ACI definition).

Cement: fine powder; reacts with water (hydration) to form glue (C-S-H) that binds aggregates.
Water: (i) chemical reaction with cement, (ii) workability. Extra water → pores → lower strength, higher permeability, poorer durability; but helps workability and prevents plastic shrinkage.
Aggregates: cheap filler, hard, give volume stability, reduce shrinkage/creep, abrasion resistance; density of concrete depends on aggregate density.
Admixtures: chemical (retarders, accelerators, water reducers, superplasticizers, air entrainers) and mineral (fly ash, silica fume, slag, RHA).

Clinker cooler (forced air; heat recovered) → ball mill grinding with gypsum → silos → bulk/bag dispatch.
Wet process: raw materials mixed with water as slurry (35–50% water) → more fuel; Dry process: less fuel, modern, most used.

Heat of hydration (highest → lowest): C₃A > C₃S > C₄AF > C₂S.
Exam point: Low-heat cement → reduce C₃A & C₃S, increase C₂S. Sulphate-resisting cement → low C₃A (≤5%). Rapid-hardening → more C₃S + finer grinding.

Concrete hardens by hydration, not by drying. Dry concrete stops gaining strength ("dry concrete = dead concrete").

Setting = change from fluid (plastic) to rigid (solid) state; mainly C₃A (and C₃S). Hardening = gain of strength after setting (C₃S, C₂S). Don't confuse the two.

Initial setting time: time from adding water until paste starts losing plasticity (Vicat needle 1 mm² fails to penetrate beyond 5 ± 0.5 mm from bottom). Must not be too short → time for mixing, transport, placing, compacting.
Final setting time: time until paste completely loses plasticity (needle with 5 mm annular collar makes an impression but collar does not). Must not be too long → early formwork removal.
Flash set: rapid irreversible stiffening due to C₃A when gypsum is insufficient; heat evolved; cannot be remixed.
False set: premature stiffening due to dehydrated gypsum (hemihydrate) recrystallising; little heat; plasticity regained by remixing without extra water.
Setting accelerated by: fineness, high C₃A, high temperature, accelerators (CaCl₂). Retarded by: gypsum, sugar, low temperature, retarders.
Approx. setting time of concrete vs temperature (cold-weather notes): 70 °F → 6 h; 60 °F → 8 h; 50 °F → 11 h; 40 °F → 14 h; 32 °F → concrete freezes.

Refractories, foundries, chemical plants, cold weather; never mix with OPC/lime

Chromium oxide → green; cobalt → blue; iron oxide → brown/red/yellow; manganese oxide → black/brown
Low heat, slow hardening, better chemical resistance, lower frost resistance
Resins, glues, sodium salts of sulphates interground

Cement in Pakistan: Mostly OPC (Type I) conforming to PS 232 / ASTM C150; sulphate-resisting cement (Type V) used in saline/coastal areas of Sindh & Balochistan; major producers include Lucky, Bestway, DG Khan and Maple Leaf.
Bag weight: Standard cement bag = 50 kg (≈ 0.035 m³, ≈ 1.25 ft³).
C₃S → early strength (first 7 days); C₂S → later strength; C₃A → flash set & sulphate attack (gypsum controls setting); C₄AF → little strength, colour.

s.t: More on this topic — Engineering Materials: Cement (Material View)
b: Raw materials: calcareous (limestone, chalk) + argillaceous (clay, shale). Gypsum (2–3%) added during grinding to retard setting.
Typical OPC oxide composition: CaO 60–67%, SiO₂ 17–25%, Al₂O₃ 3–8%, Fe₂O₃ 0.5–6%, MgO 0.1–4% (max 5–6%), SO₃ 1–3%.
Bogue compounds: C₃S (strength early, high heat), C₂S (later strength, low heat), C₃A (flash set, highest heat, sulphate attack), C₄AF (least role, colour).
Process: wet process (old) and dry process (modern, less fuel). Kiln — rotary kiln, clinker formed at ~1400–1500°C.

Standard tests: fineness (sieve 90 µm residue ≤ 10% OPC; Blaine air permeability ≥ 225 m²/kg), normal consistency (Vicat, ~25–35%), initial setting ≥ 30 min, final setting ≤ 600 min (10 hr), soundness (Le Chatelier ≤ 10 mm; autoclave ≤ 0.8%).
Compressive strength test: 1:3 cement-standard sand mortar cubes 70.6 mm (50 cm² face).

Types: Rapid hardening (more C₃S, finer), Low heat (less C₃S & C₃A; dams), Sulphate resisting (C₃A < 5%), Portland pozzolana (fly ash 15–35%), Portland slag, White cement (low iron), High alumina (refractory, very fast strength), Quick setting, Expansive, Hydrophobic, Coloured.
Unit weight of cement ≈ 1440 kg/m³; one bag = 50 kg ≈ 0.0347 m³. Specific gravity ≈ 3.15.
Aggregates occupy 60–80% of concrete volume; chemically inert fillers held by cement paste.
Fine aggregate (FA): passes No. 4 sieve (4.75 mm); sand. Coarse aggregate (CA): retained on No. 4 (> 4.75 mm; slides: > 3/8 in).
By origin: natural (river gravel, crushed rock) and artificial (slag, expanded clay, broken brick, recycled concrete).
By geology: igneous (granite, basalt), sedimentary (limestone, sandstone), metamorphic (marble, quartzite).
Insulating concrete that can be sawn/nailed
Expanded clay/shale/slate, pumice, scoria, crushed brick, expanded slag, clinker
Crushed limestone, sand, river gravel, recycled concrete
Barite, magnetite, hematite, steel/iron shot, lead shot
Shapes: rounded (river gravel), irregular, angular (crushed), flaky, elongated, flaky-and-elongated.
Rounded/smooth → better workability, less water, lower bond. Angular/rough → better bond & strength, need more paste/water.
Flakiness index: % by weight of particles whose least dimension < 0.6 × mean size. Elongation index: length > 1.8 × mean size. Both limited (commonly ≤ 15–25%).
Bond strength ↑ with surface roughness (mechanical interlock). Smaller max size → larger surface area → higher strength for given w/c.
Volume increase of damp sand due to surface moisture films; max ≈ 20–40% at ≈ 4–6% moisture; fine sand bulks more; saturated (inundated) sand shows no bulking
Total moisture − absorption; adds water to mix (adjust in mix design)
Exam point: SSD condition is the reference state in mix design — aggregate neither absorbs nor gives water to the mix.
A = SSD sample weight; B = pycnometer + sample + water; C = pycnometer + water; D = oven-dry sample.
Bulk SG (OD) = D / (C + A − B) • Bulk SG (SSD) = A / (C + A − B) • Apparent SG = D / (C + D − B)
Sample ≈ 500 g, soaked 24 ± ½ h at 22–32 °C, dried to free-running (SSD), oven 100–110 °C for 24 h.
A = weight in water (A1 − A2); B = SSD weight in air; C = oven-dry weight in air.
Bulk SG (OD) = C / (B − A) • Bulk SG (SSD) = B / (B − A) • Apparent SG = C / (C − A) • Absorption % = (B − C)/C × 100
Sample ≥ 2000 g, washed, immersed 24 h; basket dropped 25 times from 25 mm to remove air.
Grading = particle-size distribution. Well-graded aggregate → fewer voids → less paste, economy, higher strength, less segregation.
Sieve gently in varied directions; do not force material by hand; brush #50 & #100.
Fineness modulus (FM) = Σ cumulative % retained on standard sieves (#100 and coarser, incl. 3/8", ¾", 1½" for CA) ÷ 100.
FM of FA: fine sand 2.2–2.6, medium 2.6–2.9, coarse 2.9–3.2; FA with FM > 3.2 unsuitable. ASTM C33 limits FA FM to 2.3–3.1. FM of CA ≈ 6.5–8.0.
Higher FM = coarser material. FM is used in ACI 211 mix design (Table for volume of CA).
Gradation curve: sieve size (log scale, x) vs cumulative % passing (y). D10, D30, D60 = sizes at 10, 30, 60% passing.
Cu = D60 / D10 (uniformity coefficient) • Cc = (D30)² / (D10 × D60) (curvature). (The class slide wrote Cu = D60/D30 — that is a typo.)

Well graded: wide range of sizes, smooth curve, Cu > 4 (gravel) / > 6 (sand) (slide: Cu > 5), Cc 1–3. Gap graded: intermediate sizes missing (step in curve). Uniformly graded: nearly one size, steep curve, Cu ≈ 1.
Gap-graded aggregate used for exposed-aggregate finishes; needs close control to avoid segregation.
Not larger than 1/5 of narrowest dimension between forms, 1/3 of slab depth, 3/4 of clear spacing between bars (or bar & form).
Usually ≤ 1.5 in (40 mm) except mass concrete; commonly ¾"–1" (20–25 mm). Larger size → less paste & water; smaller size → higher strength at same w/c (high-strength concrete).
BS 812 / IS 2386 (lab manual lists it with C131)
Sample 12.5–10 mm; hammer 13.5–14 kg, 380 mm fall, 15 blows; AIV = (fines passing 2.36 mm / total) × 100. ≤ 45% general concrete, ≤ 30% wearing surfaces (roads, runways)
Na₂SO₄ / MgSO₄ cycles; FA loss ≤ 10% / 15%; CA ≤ 12% / 18%

Clay, silt and dust (coat aggregate → poor bond); organic matter (retards hydration); coal, lignite, mica; soft/friable particles; salts and chlorides (corrosion, efflorescence); reactive silica (ASR); sulphates.
Aggregates should be clean, hard, strong, durable; washed and screened before use.

Fineness modulus of sand: Fine sand 2.2–2.6; medium 2.6–2.9; coarse 2.9–3.2 (ASTM range 2.3–3.1). Lawrencepur sand (KP/Punjab) is a well-known high-quality sand; Margalla crush is a common coarse aggregate.
Bulking of sand: Damp sand increases in volume up to ≈ 20–30% at ≈ 4–6% moisture — correct volume batching for it.
Flakiness index: thickness < 0.6 × mean size; elongation index: length > 1.8 × mean size.

s.t: More on this topic — Engineering Materials: Aggregates & Sand
b: Sand types: pit sand (sharp, angular — best for mortar), river sand (rounded, fine — plaster), sea sand (contains salts — avoid), manufactured (crushed) sand.
Bulking of sand: increase in volume due to moisture films; max ~20–40% at about 4–6% moisture; nil for completely dry or saturated sand.
Silt content in sand should not exceed ~8% (field test: silt ≤ 8% by volume).
Shape: rounded (good workability), angular (good bond & strength), flaky/elongated (undesirable).
Tests: crushing value (≤ 30% wearing surfaces, ≤ 45% others), impact value, Los Angeles abrasion, specific gravity (~2.6–2.7), water absorption, flakiness/elongation index, soundness.
Potable water is generally suitable; must be clean, free from injurious oils, acids, alkalis, salts, sugar, organic matter (ACI 26.4.1.4; ASTM C1602).
pH commonly ≥ 6 (6–8). Sea water not used for RC/prestressed (chlorides → corrosion).
Only about 1/3 of mixing water is needed for hydration; the rest gives workability and later leaves pores.
w/c = weight of water ÷ weight of cement.
Abrams' law: for given materials and full compaction, strength depends only on w/c: f = A / B^(w/c) → lower w/c, higher strength (inverse relation).
Strength depends on w/c; economy depends on the % of aggregate that still gives a workable mix.
Typical w/c 0.4–0.6; HPC can go to 0.25 with superplasticizers.
Advantages of low w/c: higher strength, lower permeability, better weathering & freeze-thaw resistance, better bond with steel, less drying shrinkage & cracking, less volume change.
Adding water at site raises w/c: e.g., 685 lb cement, 292 lb water (w/c 0.43) + 10 gal (≈ 84 lb) water/yd³ → w/c ≈ 0.55 → big strength loss.
Gel/space ratio (Powers): strength = 240 x³ MPa (x = gel/space ratio) — strength depends on how much space hydrates fill.
Exam point: Adding water at constant cement content raises slump AND w/c (bad). To raise slump correctly, add water + cement together (constant w/c) or use a water reducer.

Fig. 17.1 — Abrams’ law: compressive strength decreases with increasing water–cement ratio.
Water needed for complete hydration ≈ 0.23–0.25 by mass plus ≈ 0.15 for gel water — total ≈ 0.38–0.42; extra water creates capillary pores.

Admixture: material other than cement, water and aggregates (and fibres) added to the batch immediately before or during mixing to modify fresh or hardened properties. Reasons: reduce cost, achieve properties more effectively, maintain quality in adverse weather, handle emergencies. No admixture substitutes for good concreting practice; always run trial mixes (compatibility with cement — C₃A content and fineness affect performance).
Reduces water ≥ 5% (typically 5–10%); lignosulfonates, hydroxylated carboxylic acids, carbohydrates
Delays set; sugar, borax, lignin, tartaric acid, gypsum, soluble zinc salts
Faster set & early strength; CaCl₂ (most common), Ca nitrite, Ca nitrate, Ca formate, triethanolamine
Flowing concrete: slump > 190 mm (7½ in) yet cohesive
Vinsol resin, synthetic detergents, sulfonated lignin, fatty acid salts
Mechanism: molecules adsorb on cement grains → same-sign surface charge → electrostatic repulsion / dispersion → released trapped water → more workability.
Uses: (i) same w/c → higher slump; (ii) same slump → lower w/c → higher strength (28-day strength 10–25% more); (iii) same strength & slump → less cement.
Plasticizers: dosage 0.1–0.4% by weight of cement, water reduction 5–15%, slump increase 3–8 cm; good plasticizer entrains < 2% air. Lignosulphonates (Ca, Na, ammonium) most common.

Superplasticizers (HRWR): sulphonated melamine formaldehyde (SMF), sulphonated naphthalene formaldehyde (SNF), modified lignosulphonates, polycarboxylate ethers (PCE) — latest. Water reduction 12–30%; strengths > 70 MPa possible; nearly no bleeding/segregation at right dose.
Effect of superplasticizer is short-lived: 30–60 min, then rapid slump loss (worse at high temperature) → often added at site.
Example: 75 mm slump + plasticizer → ~230 mm slump.
Over-dose → segregation, bleeding, excessive retardation. Higher C₃A reduces efficiency. Water reducers may slightly increase drying shrinkage; lignin-based may add 1–2% air.
Uses of flowing concrete: thin sections, congested reinforcement, tremie (under-water), pumping, places where vibration impossible.
Commercial examples in notes: Chemplast P-200 (plasticizer); Chemrite AG 200, Chemrite NN, Ultra Super Plast 437 (superplasticizers).
Delay setting; used in hot weather (concrete > 30 °C), long hauls, large pours (avoid cold joints), oil-well grouting, exposed-aggregate finishes.
Examples: sugar, borax, boric acid, lignosulphonates, tartaric acid, carbohydrate derivatives, gypsum, soluble zinc salts, MgO.
Do not lower concrete temperature; increase bleeding; may reduce 1–3-day strength; can increase rate of slump loss. Best hot-weather remedy is cooling the water/aggregates.
Speed setting & early strength; cold weather (< 5 °C / 41 °F), repairs, precast (early demoulding).

Calcium chloride (CaCl₂): cheapest, most used (esp. plain concrete). Max 2% by mass of cement; add as solution with mixing water (dry flakes → pop-outs, dark spots). Regular flake ≥ 77% CaCl₂; concentrated ≥ 94%.
Side effects: more drying shrinkage, reinforcement corrosion, darkening/discoloration, scaling. Not an anti-freeze.

Do NOT use CaCl₂ in: prestressed concrete, parking garages, concrete with embedded aluminium, reactive aggregates, sulphate exposure, dry-shake metallic floor finishes, hot weather, mass concrete. Caution: steam curing, dissimilar metals, galvanized forms, coloured concrete.
Non-chloride accelerators: calcium nitrite, calcium nitrate, calcium formate, triethanolamine, sodium thiocyanate.
Other ways to accelerate: Type III cement, extra 60–120 kg/m³ cement, water reducer, higher curing temperature.
Exam point: ACI 318 max water-soluble chloride ion (% by mass of cement): prestressed 0.06; RC exposed to chloride 0.15; RC dry/protected 1.00; other RC 0.30.
Introduce billions of microscopic, stable, uniformly distributed air bubbles (≈ 10–1000 µm; slides 10–500 µm; 0.0004–0.02 in).

Purpose: freeze–thaw durability; water expands ~9% on freezing → pushes into air voids instead of cracking paste. Also resistance to de-icer scaling, better workability, less bleeding & segregation, improved sulphate & ASR resistance.
Air content commonly 3–7% (4–8%); bubble spacing factor ≤ 0.2 mm (slide: ≤ 0.01 in).
Each 1% air ↓ compressive strength by ≈ 5%; air-entrained concrete ≈ 5% lighter; not for gravity dams where weight is needed.

Agents: Vinsol resin, Dadex, natural wood resins & soaps, animal/vegetable fats, alkali salts of sulphonated compounds, calcium lignosulphonate; gas-forming (aluminium/zinc powder, H₂O₂) give aerated concrete.
Introduced in 1930s; specs ASTM C260 (admixture), C233 (testing), C226 (for cement).
Calcium nitrite, sodium nitrite, amines, ester amines; anodic inhibitors stabilise passive film
Propylene glycol, polyoxyalkylene alkyl ether; cut drying shrinkage 25–50%
Lithium nitrate, carbonate, hydroxide; barium salts
Iron oxide, chromium oxide, cobalt blue, carbon black; ≤ 10% of cement (≤ 6% no effect); ASTM C979; avoid CaCl₂ with pigments
Calcium/ammonium stearate, butyl stearate, petroleum products — often ineffective under pressure
Latex, calcium stearate; best method: low w/c (< 0.5) + long moist curing
PVC, PVA, acrylics, SBR latex; 5–20% of cement; bond new to old concrete
Aluminium powder — slight expansion before hardening (grouts) or cellular (aerated) concrete
Tributyl phosphate, dibutyl phthalate, silicones — reduce air
Two-part stabiliser + activator; can suspend hydration up to 72 h
Cellulose ether, acrylic polymer — under-water placement without tremie
Polymers, bentonite, hydrated lime — improve pumpability
Definition: finely divided siliceous (or siliceous + aluminous) materials added in relatively large amounts, 20–70% by mass of cementitious material.

Pozzolan: siliceous/aluminous material with little or no cementing value itself, but in finely divided form reacts with Ca(OH)₂ in presence of water to form C-S-H. Name from pozzolana volcanic ash (Pozzuoli, Italy; Roman concrete = lime + volcanic ash).
Pozzolanic reaction: Ca(OH)₂ + SiO₂ + H₂O → C-S-H (consumes weak CH, refines pores).

Benefits: lower cost & energy, lower CO₂ (cement production ≈ 7–8% of world CO₂; ~1 t CO₂ per t cement), lower heat, lower permeability, higher long-term strength, better sulphate/chloride/ASR resistance, less bleeding.
Drawbacks: slower early strength, need longer curing; very fine SCMs (SF, RHA) increase water demand.
Classification: natural (volcanic ash/tuff, pumicite, diatomaceous earth, calcined clay & shale, metakaolin) and by-products/artificial (fly ash, silica fume, GGBS, rice husk ash).
Fly ash (pulverised fuel ash) — ASTM C618
Residue of powdered-coal combustion in thermal power plants, collected electrostatically from flue gases

Spherical glassy particles (cenospheres, plerospheres) ~1–100 µm; Class F (anthracite/bituminous coal): SiO₂+Al₂O₃+Fe₂O₃ ≥ 70%, low lime (< 7–10%), only pozzolanic, dose 15–30%. Class C (sub-bituminous/lignite): ≥ 50%, ~20% lime, pozzolanic + cementitious, dose 15–40%

"Ball-bearing" effect → better workability, less water, pumpability; less bleeding/segregation; longer setting; lower heat; higher ultimate strength; lower permeability; sulphate & ASR resistance; needs longer curing. Used in ≈ 50% of US ready-mix
Silica fume (micro-silica, condensed SF) — ASTM C1240
By-product of silicon & ferro-silicon alloy production (electric arc furnace fumes; quartz + coal + woodchips)
Amorphous SiO₂ > 85% (notes > 80%); SG ≈ 2.2; particles < 1 µm (avg ≈ 0.1–0.2 µm), ~100× finer than cement; surface 13,000–30,000 m²/kg; first collected Norway 1947

Very high strength (HPC), very low permeability, chloride resistance → protects steel, high bond & abrasion resistance, reduces ASR; largest effect in reducing bleeding; low slump & high early shrinkage → use with superplasticizer
Ground granulated blast furnace slag (GGBS) — ASTM C989
Molten slag from iron blast furnace (iron ore + coke + limestone/dolomite flux), rapidly quenched in water → glassy granules → ground
Latent hydraulic (cementitious when activated by CH/alkalis); replacement up to 70%; first used South Africa 1958 (notes)
Better workability, lower water demand, longer setting, less bleeding, low heat, better flexural strength, low permeability, sulphate/chloride & ASR resistance; lighter colour
Burning rice husk at 600–700 °C for ~2 h; husk = 22% of paddy (78% rice); ash ≈ 25% of husk weight
85–90% amorphous silica; highly reactive "super-pozzolan"; optimum ≈ 10% (up to 30–40%)
Higher strength, lower heat, lower chloride penetration, chemical/abrasion resistance; > 30% replacement reduces strength; unburnt RHA unsuitable
Pulverised rock & volcanic glass (< 2 mm) from explosive eruptions
With lime → pozzolanic cement; water resistance; basis of Roman concrete (lime + volcanic ash + sea water → C-A-S-H, tobermorite)
Lower permeability, better chemical resistance, higher later strength
Blast furnace slag products: granulated slag (water-quenched → GGBS), air-cooled slag (slow cooling → crushed aggregate, riprap), pelletized/expanded slag (water/steam → lightweight aggregate).

M.Sc. research (pozzolana project): pumice powder, RHA, glass waste powder replacing 0–60% cement; 20% pumice: 63.8 MPa (28 d) → 84.4 MPa (180 d); 10% RHA: +13.9% strength at 28 d; 10% glass powder: ≈ +15% at 28 d.
Workability: ease with which concrete can be mixed, transported, placed, compacted fully (100%) and finished without segregation — having regard to the mode of compaction and place of deposition.
Consistency: degree of fluidity / mobility (ability to flow); measured roughly by slump. Workability is the wider term.
Rheology: fresh concrete is a yield-stress (Bingham) fluid — yield stress governs whether it flows/fills forms; plastic viscosity governs flow speed.
Water content (main factor): more water → more fluidity but bleeding & low strength.
Mix proportions / paste content: low paste → harsh mix; high paste → rich mix (lubrication, "ball-bearing effect").
Aggregate size: larger size → less surface area → thicker paste coating → more workable (1" cube: 6 in²; split to ½" cubes: 12 in²; ¼": 24 in²).
Shape & texture: rounded/smooth > angular/rough. Grading: well graded → better.
Admixtures: plasticizers, air entrainment ↑ workability; fly ash ↑; silica fume ↓.
Also: cement content & fineness, temperature (high temp → slump loss), time/transport duration.

Frustum: bottom 200 mm, top 100 mm, height 300 mm; 3 layers each ⅓ volume; 25 strokes per layer with 16 mm × 600 mm rod; lift cone 300 mm in 5 ± 2 s; complete test within 2½ min. Types: true, shear (repeat test), collapse (very wet). Not for very dry or very wet mixes
Low workability (vibrated concrete); more sensitive than slump; agg ≤ 40 mm
CF = weight of partially compacted (free-fall from 2 hoppers) ÷ weight of fully compacted concrete. 0.78 very low, 0.85 low, 0.92 medium, 0.95 high
Time (s) for concrete to remould from slump cone shape to cylinder under vibration; more seconds = less workable
Penetration of 13.6 kg hemisphere; slump ≈ 1.5–2 × penetration
Slump flow (spread), V-funnel, L-box, U-box, J-ring
Mass sections, little reinforcement, vibrated; normal concrete 1–2"
Columns, beams, slabs, retaining walls; most mixes 2–5"
Segregation: separation of constituents so the mix is no longer uniform; caused by differences in specific gravity and size (aggregate SG 2.6–2.7, cement 3.1–3.2).
Three types: (1) coarse aggregate separates from mortar/mix; (2) cement paste separates from coarse aggregate (grout escapes); (3) water separates from mix = bleeding.

Causes: poorly graded aggregate, excess water, badly proportioned/insufficiently mixed mix, free fall > 1.5 m, long transport, under-water placing, congested reinforcement, over-vibration, leaky formwork.
Effects: honeycombing, rock pockets, sand streaks, porous layers, low density & strength, non-homogeneous mass, plastic shrinkage cracks.

Prevention: proper grading & w/c, correct handling; drop > 1.5 m through chutes/inclined belts (slope 1:3 to 1:2) or tremie; don't let concrete flow laterally; tight formwork; vibrate correct duration; air entrainment, pozzolans; remix segregated concrete before placing (not after initial set).
Bleeding: rise of mixing water to the surface as solids settle (special form of segregation, water lightest). Main cause: high w/c (≈ 0.7); also coarse cement, lack of fines, poor mixing.
Types: normal (uniform seepage over whole surface) and channel bleeding (water escapes through localised channels).
Laitance: weak, dusty layer of cement & fines carried to the top by bleeding; must be removed before next lift.

Effects: loss of homogeneity, permeability, high w/c and weak top layer, water pockets under aggregates & bars → poor bond, delayed finishing, poor pumpability, poor bond between lifts, slip-form pavement edge collapse.
Control: reduce water / lower slump, finer cement, more fines in sand, more cement, SCMs (fly ash; silica fume most effective), air entrainment, proper grading.
If bleed water rate < evaporation rate → surface dries while plastic → plastic shrinkage cracking.
Retarders increase bleeding; superplasticized mixes may bleed slightly more than control at equal w/c.

Air content: pressure method (ASTM C231), volumetric (C173), gravimetric. Unit weight/yield: ASTM C138. Setting time of concrete: penetration resistance on sieved mortar (ASTM C403). Temperature, bleeding (ASTM C232), segregation resistance, heat generation, wet analysis.
Slump loss: loss of workability with time (hydration + evaporation + absorption); worse in hot weather and with superplasticizers/retarders.
Plastic settlement cracking: cracks over reinforcement as concrete settles.
Batching: by weight (preferred, accurate ±0.1% of batch in lab) or by volume (nominal mixes, adjust for bulking).
Lab machine mixing (ASTM C192): CA + part water → start → FA, cement, rest water → mix 3 min, rest 3 min, mix 2 min. Hand mixing: cement + sand dry until uniform colour → add CA → add water.

Truck (ready-mixed) concrete (ASTM C94): 70–100 revolutions at mixing speed (6–18 rpm); agitating speed 2–6 rpm; discharge within 1½ h or before 300 revolutions. First ready-mix delivered 1913 (Baltimore).

Transporting methods: mortar pans, wheelbarrows/handcarts, buckets & cableways/ropeways, chutes, belt conveyors, skip & hoist, transit/agitator trucks, dumpers, concrete pumps (boom/line), tremie (under water), helicopter.
Placing rules: place as near as possible to final position; in uniform layers (150–450 mm); before initial set; avoid cold joints; free drop ≤ 1.5 m; don't move concrete laterally with vibrators.

Compaction (consolidation): removes entrapped air (5% voids can cut strength ~30%). Hand: rodding, ramming, tamping. Mechanical: internal (needle/immersion) vibrators (most common; insert vertically, withdraw slowly), external (form) vibrators, surface/screed vibrators, vibrating tables; also centrifugation (spun pipes/poles), pressure & jolting, vacuum dewatering.
Poor consolidation → honeycombing, early corrosion, low strength. Over-vibration → segregation, bleeding, laitance.

Fig. 19.1 — Slump cone and true, shear and collapse slump.
Compacting factor test suits low-workability mixes; Vee-Bee for very stiff mixes; flow table for high workability; slump-flow & J-ring/L-box for SCC.
Curing: maintaining satisfactory moisture and temperature in concrete for a suitable period immediately after placing & finishing so hydration continues and desired properties develop.
Two purposes: (1) retain moisture so strength keeps rising; (2) delay drying shrinkage until concrete is strong enough to resist cracking.
Factors: time, temperature, moisture. Longer curing → greater strength, lower permeability, better durability.
Concrete must not dry or freeze in the first 7–10 days; if it freezes in first 24 h it may never reach its properties. Dried concrete cannot be re-vitalised fully.
Minimum curing: ≈ 7 days for OPC (ACI/IS), ≥ 10 days with mineral admixtures or in hot/dry weather; concrete with fly ash needs longer curing.

Curing temperature: higher → faster early gain but lower ultimate strength; best ≈ room temperature (course notes: 28–32 °C range; strongest long-term at ~40 °F but impractical); > 120 °F (≈ 50 °C) harmful.
Ponding, immersion, spraying/sprinkling, fogging, wet coverings (hessian/burlap, straw, sand)
Polyethylene sheets, waterproof paper, liquid membrane-forming curing compounds
Steam curing (live steam at atmospheric pressure; high-pressure autoclave), electrical, infrared, hot-water curing
Admixtures such as polyethylene glycol (PEG), pre-wetted lightweight aggregate, SAP — useful where water is scarce
Accelerates strength; used in precast/prestressed elements (girders, slabs, piles, blocks).
Live steam (atmospheric, ~14 psi): max 40–100 °C, optimum 65–80 °C; higher initial temperature → lower ultimate strength.
Cycle: (1) delay/presetting period, (2) heating period, (3) maximum temperature period, (4) cooling period.

Advantages: 24-h strength ≈ 28-day normal strength; less creep & shrinkage; better sulphate resistance; no efflorescence; quality control. Disadvantages: costly set-up, not in-situ, unsuitable for large surfaces, skilled labour; CaCl₂ to be used with caution.

s.t: 7.3 Strength gain with age (Type I, moist cured — ACI 209)
b: About 90% of strength develops in first 28 days; concrete continues gaining strength for years if moist.
ACI 209: f'c(t) = f'c(28) × t / (4 + 0.85t) for Type I moist cured.
Maximum resistance to axial compressive load per unit area; tested at 28 days (also 7 days); expressed in psi or MPa.
Specimens: cylinder 150 × 300 mm (6 × 12 in) (ASTM C39, ACI), cube 150 mm (BS/IS; 100 mm if max aggregate ≤ 20 mm), cores (ASTM C42). L/D of cylinder = 2.
Cubes tested on cast sides (not top/bottom), no packing; loading ≈ 140 kg/cm²/min (≈ 14 MPa/min; ASTM C39: 0.25 ± 0.05 MPa/s). At least 3 specimens per age.
Most structural concrete: 3000–5000 psi (20–35 MPa); high-rise columns up to 12,000–15,000 psi.
High-strength concrete (ACI 363): f'c ≥ 8000 psi (55 MPa). HPC (class notes): 10,000–15,000 psi, w/c ≈ 0.25.
w/c ratio (most important; inverse — Abrams). Degree of compaction (voids/porosity). Curing (time, temperature, humidity). Age.

Cement: type (Type III high early), fineness, composition, content (direct relation). Aggregate: strength, texture, shape, grading, size, cleanliness, aggregate/cement ratio (strength ↑ as a/c decreases to ~2).
Air content (inverse). Admixtures. Test conditions: specimen shape & size, moisture & temperature of specimen (wet specimens test lower), loading rate (faster → higher), end conditions/capping.
150 × 300 mm cylinder, ASTM C496; 3 mm plywood strips 25 mm wide; load rate 0.7–1.4 MPa/min
T = 2P / (π L D) ; fct ≈ 6.7 √f'c psi (≈ 0.56 √f'c MPa)
150 × 150 × 700 mm beam (100 × 100 × 500 if agg ≤ 19 mm); 6 × 6 × 30 in; ASTM C78; load lines 20 cm (or 13.3 cm) apart

Effects: cracking when restrained (tension > tensile strength), opens joints, tile debonding, extra deflection, prestress loss; improves grip on bars (bond). Prevention: low water, max aggregate, early curing, shrinkage reducers, joints, sun shades, dampen sub-grade (not over-wet).
Creep: time-dependent increase in strain under sustained (constant) load; instantaneous (elastic) strain occurs first, then creep.
On unloading: instantaneous recovery + creep recovery, leaving residual (permanent) deformation. Total creep = basic creep + drying creep.
Creep strain = φ × elastic strain (φ = creep coefficient ≈ 1.5 – 4; higher when loaded young: ~3.7 at 7 days vs ~1.4 at 1 year).
In beams, long-term creep deflection can be ≈ 2 × initial elastic deflection; compression steel controls creep.

Factors (↑ creep): higher w/c, more/poorer paste, lower strength, young age at loading, poor curing, low humidity, higher stress (creep ∝ stress; no lower limit), higher temperature (up to ~70 °C), lightweight/low-E aggregate, admixtures & pozzolans. Aggregate itself hardly creeps — it restrains paste.

Effects: increased deflection of beams, buckling of eccentric columns, loss of prestress, stress redistribution; beneficial: relieves restrained shrinkage & thermal stresses. Harmful in dams (internal cracking). Test: ASTM C512.
High-strength concrete: shrinkage ≈ normal concrete; creep coefficient considerably less.
Concrete is the most fire-resistant structural material, but strength & E fall and creep rises at high temperature; steel protected by cover.

Durability: ability of concrete to resist weathering, chemical attack, abrasion and other deterioration while performing satisfactorily in its environment for its design life.
Internal causes: alkali–aggregate reaction, volume changes (thermal incompatibility of aggregate & paste), permeability, corrosion of steel.
External causes: physical (freeze–thaw, abrasion, temperature extremes, weathering), chemical (sulphates, chlorides, acids, leaching, sea water, CO₂), mechanical, electrolytic.
Three most common problems (ACI): corrosion of steel, freeze–thaw breakdown, chemical attack (ACI 318 Chapter 19 gives exposure classes & limits).
For durable concrete: low w/c, adequate cement content, full compaction, proper curing, adequate cover, suitable cement (SRC, PBFC, PPC), SCMs, good workmanship, low permeability.
Excess mixing water; freeze at −1 to −8 °C; govern permeability & frost damage
Water expands ≈ 9% on freezing; damage when concrete is critically saturated (≈ 91% of pores filled).
Mechanisms: hydraulic pressure (unfrozen water forced through capillaries), osmotic pressure, capillary ice growth.
Signs: scaling, spalling, D-cracking, pop-outs, crumbling at joints. Locations: pavements, bridge decks, retaining walls in cold climates.
De-icing salts (NaCl, CaCl₂; formates) make it more severe (osmotic pressure, saturation) → surface scaling + rebar corrosion.
Prevention: air entrainment (4–8%), low w/c, proper curing, frost-resistant aggregate, allow drying before first freeze.
Alkalis (Na⁺, K⁺, OH⁻ from cement) + reactive silica in aggregate + moisture → alkali-silica gel which absorbs water and swells: SiO₂ + 2NaOH + H₂O → Na₂SiO₃·2H₂O.
Gel forms at the aggregate–paste transition zone; expansion > tensile strength → cracking; at the surface → map (pattern) cracking; also pop-outs, gel exudation, loss of strength & stiffness.
Theories: absorption-swelling and osmotic pressure. Needs RH ≥ ~75–80%. Common in dams, piers, sea walls, pavements.

Prevention: low-alkali cement (Na₂O eq ≤ 0.6%), limit cement content & external alkalis (sea water, de-icers), non-reactive aggregate, limit moisture, SCMs (fly ash, GGBS, silica fume, volcanic glass), lithium admixtures, air entrainment (room for gel). Alkali–carbonate reaction is a related type with dolomitic limestone.
Sulphate ions (Na, K, Mg, Ca sulphates) from soils, groundwater, sea water, sewage, industrial waste react with hydration products:
CH + sulphate → gypsum; C₃A hydrates (monosulphate) + gypsum → ettringite (calcium sulpho-aluminate) — large volume increase → expansion & cracking.
Na₂SO₄ + CH + 2H → CaSO₄·2H₂O + 2NaOH (alkalinity maintained, C-S-H stable).
Magnesium sulphate is most aggressive: forms insoluble Mg(OH)₂, lowers pH, attacks C-S-H itself → mushy, non-cohesive mass.
Signs: cracking & expansion starting at edges and corners; whitish surface; ettringite in cracks/voids.
Prevention: dense low-permeability concrete (low w/c), limit C₃A — Type II (≤ 8%) or Type V (≤ 5%)/SRC, pozzolans/GGBS (for > 1500 mg/L sulphate), protective coatings.
Steel is protected by high pH (> 12) passive oxide film and concrete cover. Chlorides (or carbonation) destroy passivity → rust (volume ↑ 2–6×) → cracking, spalling, loss of bond & section.
Chloride attack is responsible for ≈ 40% of concrete structural failures (class presentation).
Internal sources: sea water in mixing, CaCl₂ accelerator, unwashed/salty aggregates. External: sea water, de-icing salts, stored chemicals.

Prevention: more cover (+1 inch cover can roughly double service life), low permeability (low w/c, SCMs), corrosion inhibitors (Ca nitrite), epoxy-coated/galvanized/stainless-clad bars, cathodic protection, chloride limits (ACI table in 5.4).
CO₂ from air + Ca(OH)₂ (with moisture) → CaCO₃; lowers pore pH from ~12.5 to < 9 → depassivates steel within carbonated depth.
Rate ↑ with permeability, high w/c, poor curing; fastest at RH ≈ 50–70%. Lightweight concrete: carbonation depth ≈ 2 × normal → more cover.
Test: phenolphthalein spray — pink = uncarbonated (alkaline), colourless = carbonated.
